title: Rare Disease Diagnosis
answer: Rare disease diagnosis uses AI to search genomic sequences, clinical notes, and phenotype descriptions for patterns that match known rare conditions. The work spans variant calling, gene prioritization, and differential diagnosis support for clinicians who may see only a handful of cases in a career. It covers both germline and somatic rare disorders, and increasingly includes undiagnosed disease programs where standard testing has failed.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Rare disease diagnosis uses AI to search genomic sequences, clinical notes, and phenotype descriptions for patterns that match known rare conditions. The work spans variant calling, gene prioritization, and differential diagnosis support for clinicians who may see only a handful of cases in a career. It covers both germline and somatic rare disorders, and increasingly includes undiagnosed disease programs where standard testing has failed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on secure hospital or cloud compute with access to reference genomes, variant databases, and electronic health records. They require high throughput sequencing pipelines, GPU or CPU clusters for model inference, and controlled data environments that meet clinical data protection rules. Many deployments sit behind institutional firewalls because raw genomic data is sensitive and large.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining phenotype extraction from clinical text with genomic variant interpretation. Models rank candidate genes by comparing a patient's symptoms, encoded as Human Phenotype Ontology terms, against known gene to phenotype associations. Some systems use facial analysis from photographs, others use knowledge graphs or large language models to read clinician notes, but the core task is always to narrow a long list of variants to a short list of plausible diagnoses for human review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on patient consent, data provenance, and the possibility of false reassurance or missed diagnoses. Genomic data is identifying and often shared across institutions, so access controls and audit trails matter. Product liability questions are live in this field, and a clinician remains responsible for any diagnosis, with AI output treated as a decision support tool rather than a final answer.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward earlier diagnosis in newborns and better integration with standard electronic health record workflows. Work is underway on models that can propose therapies or clinical trials once a rare disease is identified, and on federated learning so hospitals can improve models without moving patient data. The main open challenge is validating these tools across diverse populations where rare disease presentation and genetic background differ.
